In 1911 Freud denounced Adler in two papers presented before the Vienna Society; soon after, Adler and Stekel resigned their offices to form their own psychoanalytic society, The Society for Free Psychoanalysis. Adler had strayed too far from Freudian theory. He deemphasized the role of libido and the unconscious in the etiology of neurosis, focusing instead on the role of aggression and ego mechanisms.

Two years later, at the Congress of 1913, the long-simmering dispute between Freud and Jung surfaced outright. Freud could no longer tolerate the large theoretical discrepancy between the psychoanalysis he founded and the psychoanalysis Carl Jung was formulating. Jung's concept of the libido differed vastly from Freud's, and the stress Jung placed on current conflicts contradicted the importance of childhood factors in the organization and formation of neuroses, which Freud had labored hard to establish. Psychoanalysis had become unrecognizable in the hands of Jung.

Over seventy years have elapsed since then, and in that time psychoanalysis has sufficiently fixed itself in the cultural fabric. What Freud fought hard to nurture and protect has been widely accepted. His foundling science no longer needs such a zealous and tenacious guardian: it is now strong enough to support variant theories without the threat of rupture.

Ann Jones is right about so much, it seems petty to quibble over one point. But quibble I will-not because it is one of the first very points she makes-but because it is the precise reason I selected her book: Jones writes that murder stories and murder books are only

230

with exception not serious attempts at understanding the phenomenon of murder.

It is not an accident that I have been reading true-life murder stories for as long as I have been reading psychoanalysis. It did not take me long to realize that books about murder, when well done, had simply the best psychological analyses of character and character formation around-and, of course, were infinitely more readable, enjoyable, and entertaining than the dry language of psycho-analyzese. The fact that I was reading about impulses translated into fatal behavior, rather than the rarified abstractness of a neurotic psyche merely turning on itself was never much of a distinction for me. Murder is murder in the unconscious, whether it is physical or psychological, and whether it is turned against the self or another.

I always knew intuitively that murder committed by a woman was different than the same act committed by a man. But the rarity of that event, and the even more infrequent writing on female murderesses, left my impression as only an idea. So, it is a particularly welcome event that Ann Jones has combined both of my rather obsessive interests in this volume. And, finally, for just one last reason that Jones's book should be required reading for any serious student of the human psyche, she remembers that the implementation of drives-not the urge to kill, but the decision to act on that urge-and our social response to that act, is made within a broader social context. Her book, as does any good true-life murder story, views historical and social forces as variables interacting with the psychological drives and conflicts.

This book is a series of stories about womens' homicides. Each selection was a prominent case, and received a fair amount of publicity in its day. With some of the more recent, we will even remember our own preoccupation with the case when it reached the newsstands, including Alice Crimmins, Candy Mossier, and, in the paperback edition, Jean Harris. The fact that the cases chosen were much talked about, some even previously written about, is certainly telling evidence that social and personal nerves were hit. The women I know, including myself (and including Ann Jones), did not rush out each morning in November 1980 to glean the latest newspaper gossip of Jean Harris's trial for lack of identification. The jealousy given rise to by that love triangle was something a lot of us knew about firsthand. The pursuit of a man who gave us just enough encouragement to continue the chase, but not enough to calm us into sighing deeply, was something most of us could identify with.

“In many cases,” Freud writes in his Leonardo da Vinci, “they [biographers] have chosen their hero as the subject of their studies because—for reasons of their personal emotional life—they have felt a special affection for him from the very first.” In many cases, but not in all. Of late there has beeen a proliferation of studies of Freud whose authors can lay little claim to special affection for their subject. Whether the study was undertaken with the alleged purpose of portraying the subject life-size with all his strengths and weaknesses, so that he be seen objectively, or whether for the sake of “historical truth,” the result is often lamentably the same: a form of character assassination. It is a relief, therefore, to read a study of Freud whose author has no psychological ax to grind. Peter Gay is not to be numbered among the purveyors of “correct” portraiture or “historical truth.” He has, refreshingly, tamed his unruly subterranean impulses. There is no doubt that Gay harbors a special affection for his subject, but his affection does not seem to blunt his judgment or blur his vision. He does not seem to hesitate to disagree, to point out what he judges to be weaknesses, whether in the theory under discussion or in the man. As both a cultural historian and one conversant with psychoanalysis (he is a graduate of the Western New England Institute for Psychoanalysis), Gay is on familiar ground in both fields, and so brings to his task a rare union of expertise. An added dividend is his discursive style of writing, with its wit, informality, and easy flow, so that he who runs may read.

Note that the title of this book, Sigmund Freud's Christian Unconscious, is a statement, not a question. Convinced that Freud was deeply ambivalent about all things religious and about Christianity in particular, the author leaves no stone unturned in his search for avidence for his hypothesis that Freud had deeply buried religious feelings. Indeed, while accepting the skeptical and atheistic aspect of Freud's thought, his goal is to demonstrate that Freud, who had at times referred to himself as a Godless Jew, a Natural atheist, and hopeless pagan, had actually been strongly influenced by Christian ideas.

Following Freud's own methods of psychoanalytic investigation and using Freud's own words and constructions in exploring his life, writings, and dreams, Vits traces Freud's development and examines how he was influenced by religion during various phases of his life. He stresses what he sees as the great lasting influence of Freud's Catholic nanny—his beloved primary caretaker until she mysteriously “disappeared” fromm the household when he was three years old. Vitz is convinced that Freud's sorrow and pessimism can be traced to the loss of this nanny and the “Eden” of Freiberg.

Vitz notes that such autobiographical elements are often parts of the underpinnings of Freud's theories and the takes a long look at what he thinks Freud is telling us about himself in his theories and case histories. He traces references to Christian themes in Freud's work and points out the similarity of some Christion concepts to some of Freud's own theorizing. He attempts to reconcile this influence with Freud's belief that religion is an illusion.

Alzheimer's Disease has become a familiar and fearful diagnosis for many older adults during the last decade. A very debilitating disease, its effects extend far beyond the devastation experienced by the patient: it strains the emotional and practical resources of the victim's family and friends. While the cause of Alzheimer's Disease remains unknown and treatment is limited, much research and clinical work is in progress. Possible means of symptom amelioration and more effective methods of managing these neurologically impaired older adults are being studied. There is hope for breakthroughs in both treatment and prevention in the near future.

For the most part, the literature on this syndrome is devoted to identifying symptoms and understanding the behavioral changes of the declining patient: less attention has been paid to the needs of the primary caregivers, who need guidance in management techniques and coping strategies to use during the progression of the disorder. Caring for the Alzheimer Patient: A Practical Guide offers comprehensive and practical information for the caregiver, who is usually a member of the family. The chapters are authored by experts in the health care professions and related fields, and focus on the provision of comfort and quality care. The book cover a wide range of topics, which fall into four major categories: managing the medical, physical, and psychological problems of the patient; supporting the psychological well-being of the caregiver; effective utilization of community resources; and ethical and legal considerations.

The authors emphasize the need to reduce the level of stress for both the patient and the caregiver. They discuss how education, counseling, therapy, and support groups can be very helpful.

Alana London

Alana London

One Ascan Avenue
Forest Hills, NY 11375

Alana London   Graduate of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies and is in practice in New York City. She serves as a Fellow at the CMPS Referral Service. She is also a member of the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis and The Society of Modern Psychoanalysts.

Analysts working with narcissistic transference frequently find that the treatment has hopelessly foundered, the patient has been “lost somehow,” that they themselves have developed disturbing symptoms, or even that their own personal lives have become seriously disrupted. It is now understood that these phenomena are often linked to the presence of unresolved narcissistic countertransference resistances.

The modern analytic supervisor recognizes the fact that the supervisee may become resistant to the supervision itself when exploration of the case process stimulates awareness of the therapist's own impulses. This resistance may be analogous to the countertransference resistance the supervisee has developed in the analytic relationship with the patient. As the resistance is experienced, explored, analyzed and resolved in the supervisory relationship, the supervisee develops the ability to have the thoughts and feelings necessary to relate therapeutically to the patient.

I had occasion to learn about this process first hand, when I found myself compulsively repeating in the relationship with my supervisor what my narcissistically disturbed patient was repeating in the analytic relationship with me. Belief that I was in the grip of a powerful induction did nothing to release me. The resistance was resolved only when I got to the root of it in a resistance to my own analysis which blocked the feelings needed in my work with the patient.

The resistance to supervision and countertransference resistance to the patient contained the same emotional structure—both served to defend against impulses I was not free to work through in analysis.

197

Ronald Lieber

Ronald Lieber  

On a Sunday afternoon in January 1908, a squat, cherubic, bespectacled man, Sandor Ferenczi, stood before the wooden door of Berggasse 19. He was accompanied by Dr. Stein, a slight acquaintance of Freud, who provided the formal introduction. Ferenczi was a recent convert to the new psychoanalytic science, having just reread

226

The Interpretation of Dreams, and was determined to meet its author. The outcome of that Sunday encounter could have turned out like innumerable other introductions of such sort, a mannered, perhaps strained conversation, and then goodbye, another brief but innocuous engagement, another name. Those meetings leave little for history. But Ferenczi and Freud struck a mutual chord and left behind traces of a professional and personal friendship that would both exert a distinct influence on the development of the foundling science and leave on one of its participants an indelible mark. Ferenczi was invited back for a two-week stay in August.

Freud was drawn to Ferenczi's lively, inquisitive mind, which mirrored a tendency that Freud struggled all his life to tame and discipline. Every topic drew an animated response. The two would talk long into the night, each prodding the other to further speculation. Usually it was Freud who watched Ferenczi's ecstatic intuitions soar beyond his conjectures. The nearly 2500 letters Freud wrote to Ferenczi attest to his admiration and affection for the new disciple. At one time Freud expressed the wish that Mathilde, his eldest daughter, marry Ferenczi, and he even went so far as to address him a “My Dear Son”-the sentiment of which was not lost on Ferenczi, whose need for intimacy would never be sated. Yet the irony remains: those aspects of Ferenczi's character which drew him close to Freud ultimately fueled the schism.

Freud analyzed Ferenczi in two brief stints during 1914 and 1916, but the transference was never resolved; its positive aspect was encouraged and exacerbated by their personal and professional contact. Freud, the leader and final arbiter of psychoanalytic matters, could not help but assume the central and fatherly position that Ferenczi thrust upon him. It is to that figure Ferenczi was tethered. In a 1922 correspondence Ferenczi writes of making a gift to Freud of “overtender and oversensitive emotions appropriate to my physical father.” Yet Freud could not possibly gratify the transferential needs, and he increasingly confronted the role Ferenczi insisted he play. The more distant Freud seemed to grow, the more fired became Ferenczi's unanswered desires. And a lingering resentment, never before acknowledged, was mobilized. As late as 1930, three years before his death, Ferenczi would accuse Freud of not having dealt with the negative transference.

Authors are a sensitive lot, prey to the adjectival productions of their reviewers. Freud, as is well known, was no exception. Over the years opinions have ranged on both sides on the question of whether Freud and his ideas were appreciated in his own time. This has been especially true since the attempt of Bry and Rifkin (1962) to show that opposition was less sustained than Freud imagined. Kiell retrieved 800 items in German, French, and English, and has selected for this volume 172 reviews of 39 works by Freud, including 32 reviews of The Interpretation of Dreams. Kiell tells us something about each critic and gives a summary of the review, which is then printed in full. He often includes a cogent explanation of the topic of the review, placing it within its theoretical context in psychoanalysis. In the course of reading through this book one also attains an impression of the social milieu and the state of psychology contemporaneous with each work. We are indebted to Kiell for this wonderful addition to scholarship about Freud. This collection will also delight those with a penchant for entering unknown byways as they dip into dictionaries and encyclopedias at odd moments and respond to both the familiar and the unexpected.

I would certainly recommend this slim but inspired volume to anyone who would like to encounter many of our modern analytic ideas coming from a person who has apparently arrived at them independently, and who presents them in a fresh, charming, and lucid manner.

Havens describes a case where providing a safe environment seemed hopeless: “His was a vehicle so tightly sealed that even the windows were black; I had no idea what to do.” “I was a blind surgeon, a blind umpire, not knowing what was sensitive, what was tough, where he hurt, what he enjoyed. I felt it would have been the easiest thing in the world to drive this man mad or at least drive him away.” The patient had previously been with an analyst (presumably classical). “At the end he had been hospitalized with what he said was psychosis. So silence and neutrality did not constitute a safe place for him.” Havens found a way out, but his task would have been made easier by “contact functioning” and by other modern psychoanalytic techniques.

Many of the ideas (but not the techniques) promulgated by Spot-nitz and his colleagues a generation ago now seem to be appearing in the works of people who are outside the modern analytic school—particularly the need for a safe, ego-syntonic environment.

Problems of Insight in Psychoanalysis

Oscar Sternbach

Oscar Sternbach

12 West 96th St.
New York, N.Y. 10025

Oscar Sternbach   Started his psychoanalytic studies in Vienna and came to this country in 1939. He has been a psychoanalyst in private practice for many years. He has also been on the faculties of several psychoanalytic institutes, among them the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. He is the author of a number of articles about theory and technique of adult-and child-psychoanalysis.

The question of “insight” in psychoanalysis is related to the primal psychoanalytic aim of seeking to make the unconscious conscious again. For the classical analyst “insight” is the essence of psychoanalysis. Practically the term insight has in America come to be used to indicate that one is conscious of one's unconscious. A classical psychoanalyst “gives insight” to the patient by interpretation or reconstruction. The analysand then “arrives at insight” as a consequence of being given insight by his analyst. Occasionally the patient himself has an insight independently or autonomously. In this connection the questions “what does it mean to be conscious” and “when can one say that the unconscious has become conscious” are legitimate enough to justify a serious investigation, although at the first glance they may seem to be utterly superfluous. The terms conscious and unconscious are used by everybody with a nonchalance that denies they could be problematic. If we know anything-don't we know it when we are conscious of something?

In 1952, Gregory Zilboorg, then a somewhat controversial author in the forties and fifties, discussed the meaning of insight in an article published in the Psychoanalytic Quarterly, “The Emotional Problem and the Therapeutic Role of Insight.” He says there that:

Among the unclarities which are of utmost clinical importance and which cause utmost confusion is the term insight. It came from nowhere, so to speak. No one knows who employed it first, and in what sense … in the course of the last thirty or forty years it has undergone so many changes and shifts that the concept has become even less clear….

Although there are finer creations of the spirit than perversion and psychosis, in the long run it is better to be mad than dead.

Joyce McDougall

In observing the ways in which the process of differentiation between self and not-self can be thwarted on the level of the mind, Freud identified the disease of pathological narcissism. Parallel scientific research on the level of the body revealed that the equivalent somatic dysfunction led to the disease of cancer. Each of these two conditions reflects a state of dedifferentiation where the normally distinct boundaries between self and not-self are blurred.

Freud's psychosexual phases of development formulate a normal progression towards psychosexual maturity. If early stages of development are not mastered, the personality remains stuck—fixated—at an early level of functioning. When fixation occurs before self and not-self separate and become distinct from one another, the consequences are quite severe. While physical maturity may proceed, the narcissistic adult remains an emotional child housed in an adult body (alongside an adult intellect, often enough). Primary narcissism, a normal developmental phase in early infancy, is now pathological narcissism—a self/object fusion that is no longer appropriate.

Alternatively, differentiation may have occurred, but the original self/not-self fusion reappears regressively in dedifferentiation.

Psychoanalysis is a tripartite system of investigation—at once a system of research, a system of therapy, and a system of understanding human development. This paper consists of reflections on the creative and destructive forces in human development, viewed from a psychoanalytic perspective and in the light of the dual drives. It will refer to the three systems of investigation as observed in case studies and in theoretical postulations.

The early analytic theroists were concerned with questions that had been pondered for millennia before them and that still confront us today. They were addressing the creative and destructive forces in human development—the vital forces of sexuality and aggression—in an attempt to understand their impact on human behaviour. From these pursuits grew a language and a science whose evoltion continues in our own time (Ellenberger, 1970).

Fredud's theories on sexuality, the creative force, were profound and far-reaching. Because they were so strongly resisted, however, Freud spent a great part of his professional life contending with his detractors. He ascribed the resistance that met his theories of sexuality to society's collective inability to overcome its own repressions of sexual strivings, impulses, and wishes. Although infant sexuality was observable and evident, he felt that adult observers were inclined to deny it; and that, in fact, they ojected forcefully to recognizing sexuality as normal developmental functioning. Freud (1913) believed that the taboo of incest was—and is—at the heart of this resistance.

In Freud's later years (1930) he came to recognize and to begin to account for aggression and the destructive force in human development.

In order to highlight the modern psychoanalytic perspective on maladaptive family ties, I shall begin by presenting a clinical vignette that illustrates some of the pitfalls of a more traditional approach.

An advanced candidate in one of the institutes in which I supervise, shortly after beginning supervision, came into the session very upset about something that had happened earlier in the day, during a session with one of his patients.

The patient, an attractive, appealing woman of 25 years, had begun treatment with him on a twice-a-week basis about two months before. She had had no previous experience with therapy. She said that she felt frustrated with her life situation. She was getting no place in her career and had been unable to develop a satisfactory, enduring relationship with a man.

Although she had no difficulty in attracting and meeting men, she found most men too weak for her taste, and those to whom she became attracted were either married, in some other way unavailable, or ultimately abusive.

She had droppedl out of college owing to insufficient interest in academics. She wanted a career in business but somehow was not able to progress beyond the position of office manager.

What do men want?

The first person that I asked that question said, “Everybody knows that!”

I said, “What?”

He said, “Sex!”

The second person that I asked said, “Everybody knows that!”

I said, “What?”

He said, “A mother!”

A mother is only brought unlimited satisfaction by her relationship to her son; this is altogether the most perfect, most free from ambivalence of all human relationships. A mother can transfer to her son the ambition she has been obliged to suppress in herself, and she can expect from him the satisfaction of all that has been left over in her of her masculinity complex.

Freud

Freud was born in a caul. This unusual circumstance was a source of great delight to his mother, Amalia, for according to folklore a child so born was destined to a life of happiness and fame. In quick succession, seven additional children were born (the second, Julius, died in infancy). Of her seven surviving children, Sigmund, her first-born, remained Amalia's favorite: mein goldener Sigi, Sigi, mein Gold. Amalia's belief that Sigmund was destined to greatness was reinforced by the prophecy of an old woman she met in a pastry shop. “It became one of the constantly repeated family stories, a part of the atmosphere in which the child grew up. Thus the hero's garb was in the weaving, right at the cradle” (Bernfeld, 1940/1973, p. 189). “Could this,” Freud asks himself, “have been the source of my thirst for grandeur?” (1900, Standard Edition, 4: 192). Could Freud, master solver of riddles, have seriously asked this question? Perhaps it was his sister Anna who more accurately identified the source of her brother's thirst for grandeur. “My mother,” writes Anna Freud Bernays (1940/1973)

Psychoanalysis…never shuts the door on a new truth

Freud

This article attempts to spell out the steps to be taken and the areas in which to take them, by way of supplementing the modern analytic research principles set forth by Meadow (1981, 1984) in earlier issues of this journal. Freud (1987, p. 83) has described scientific creativity as “the succession of daringly playful fantasy and relentlessly realistic critisism”-in other words, an interplay of primary and secondary process. Under these conditions, rationality is intermittently suspended, ego boundaries are similarly rendered permeable, while the final esthetic derives from the merging of form and substance. In the psychoanalytic context, scientific creativity is fueled by curiosity about psychic process, and in the best of worlds the aim is to attain a state of illumination which goes by the name of meaning. In more mundance clinical circumstances, the artist strives to be something of a scientist, and the scientist something of an artist, the two joining hands to guide the healer toward his incremental therapeutic successes.

If we apply this line of thought to the actualities of clinical psychoanalysis, we find ourselves caught up in a web crosshatched of received wisdom and open-ended potentialities. And who is to say where the one ends and the other begins? We do, however, owe ourselves a debt of attentiveness to fact, fancy and affect, as they invest the mind's eye.

This book is an ambitious undertaking successfully executed. Beginning with Freud, who emphasized the vital role of transference in psychoanalysis but dealt with countertransference dismissively, as something to be “overcome,” the Marshalls trace the growing recognition of the importance of the transference-countertransference interaction in therapy. This is no mean task. It involves not only identifying the many types of transference and countertransference and their mutations, antecedents, and consequences, but also establishing a coherent schema for determining their place in the ever-shifting phases of the therapeutic process. In Freud's metaphor, (“… where I have discovered a few temples, others may discover a continent.”), this work by the Marshalls may be said to contribute significantly toward the evolutionary process of discovery.

The scholarship that went into the writing of this book is impressive. The input from all the main psychoanalytic orientations to an understanding of the concepts of transference and countertransference is outlined and evaluated. The authors then lucidly present their own contribution—but not as mere theorizing. Their aim is to guide the therapist and supervisor operationally out of the morass of definitions and conflicting concepts to an appreciation of the transference-countertransference forces at work in the therapy setting. In the process, they highlight the preeminent role of feelings in patient-analyst-supervisor interactions.

Re-analysis After the Death of the Analyst: The Problem of Countertransference in Re-analysis

Gisela Tauber J.D.

Gisela Tauber

240 East 76th St.
New York, N.Y. 10021

Gisela Tauber   Received her degree in Criminal Psychology from the University of Prague and is currently a psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. She has taught at NPAP and NYCPT and has lectured extensively on adult-and child-psychoanalysis. She is the author of many papers, including a psychoanalytic study of Thomas Jefferson.

I was struck by certain developments in the re-analyses of two women patients who both came to me after the death of their female analysts. Both of the analysts had died after long illnesses.

Effect of the Trauma of Death in Re-analysis

The attitudes and behavior of these two patients displayed some unusual similarities which, although the patients were dissimilar in many ways, distinguished them from other of my re-analysands. I soon found myself under a peculiar strain, which I came to realize was due to these patients' persistent comparison of anything I did, said, or omitted to say, with their dead analyst. Evidently, I was found to be wanting in all regards.

Consciously I was aware that both these women needed consolation and support, but I also knew that pampering them would worsen their depressions (No rachmones, as Theodor Reik used to say). Under their constant barrage of rageful criticism, which I felt had to be directed against their dead analysts for abandoning them, I began to doubt myself. I wondered whether I was feeling some unconscious sense of victory since I was alive and their analysts-one of whom was my friend and mentor-were dead. Under the impact of their anger I wondered whether they might have a point. Maybe I really was a miserable analyst-not as wise or compassionate as their former analysts. Maybe I envied the former analysts. What qualities in them made these women love them so much, when they reacted to me by wanting to tear me to pieces?

Phyllis Meadow PHD

Phyllis Meadow

245 West 13th St.

Phyllis Meadow   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City and Boston. She is a founder and Chair of the Board of Trustees of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies, and the Executive Director of the Boston Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. She is also a founder and former President of the National Accreditation Association for Psychoanalysis. She has served on the Board of Directors of the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis as Membership Director. Her publications include Treatment of the Narcissistic Neuroses, co-authored with Hyman Spotnitz; a monograph, Emotional Education: The Theory and Process of Training Psychoanalysts. Among her many published papers are “Drive Theory and Diagnosis in Treatment,” “The Myth of the Impersonal Analyst,” “Object Relations in a Drive Theory Model.”

Historical Perspective

1976 saw the publication of two texts, one by Hyman Spotnitz, Psychotherapy of Preoedipal Conditions, and one by Hyman Spotnitz and Phyllis W. Meadow, Treatment of the Narcissistic Neuroses. These volumes updated modern analytic thinking on the treatment of narcissistic disorders, including Spotnitz's special interest in the psychotic character structure. My contribution to the second volume was to prepare two chapters on theoretical considerations, “Dream analysis” and “Diagnosis re-evaluated,” and three chapters on technical considerations, “The treatment partnership,” “The analyst intervenes,” and “A case study,” on what happens between patient and analyst to bring about change. The conclusions: Only when the analyst can help the narcissistic patient develop an emotional relationship, in other words, a transference, can the patient be cured by analytic work. It is the emotional connection with the analyst that helps the patient to stay in treatment when feelings are painful; establishing that connection means overcoming powerful resistances.

Today I would like to update my thinking on how I try to be with patients, and perhaps say something about why I believe that this approach works. Also I would like to mention briefly the history of modern psychoanalysis and give those who are not familiar with modern psychoanalysis, some idea about what it is. Spotnitz's work in the late forties with adolescent girls, mothers, and children led to his first theory: that the fragile ego needs to be insulated in the analytic sessions and that this cannot necessarily be accomplished by kindness and supportive interventions.

A Secure Base: Parent-Child Attachment and Healthy Human Development. John Bowlby. New york: Basic Books, 1988.

Richard Cheney

Richard Cheney

Richard Cheney  

While the Oedipus complex is the centerpiece of Freudian theory, Bowlby emphasizes instead the importance of the child's tie to his mother, which he view as “the resultant of a distinctive and in part pre-programmed set of behavior patterns which in the ordinary expectable environment devlop during the early months of life.” He was awakened to the possible existence of this phenomenon by Lorenz's early studies of the bonding behavior of ducks and goslings.

Bowlby argues that such early behavior patterns in humans, which he calls “attachment behaviour,” affect the ongoing behavior of both the infant and the parenting figures, irrespective of the age of the parties concerned. If the relationship between the individual attached and the attachment figure is going well, there is joy and a sense of security; if it is threatened, there is jealousy, anxiety, and anger; if broken, there is grief and depression. How such attachment behavior comes to be organized within an individual is dependent upon his early experiences both within his family and outside of it. Bowlby suggests that the role of parents should be to provide a secure base from which a child or adolescent can make sorties into the outside world and to which he can return, knowing that he will be welcomed when he gets there, that he will be nourished physically and emotionally comforted if distressed, that he will be reassured if frightened—but with his parents intervening actively only when clearly necessary.

This book explores the mechanisms of human attachment, its implications for lifelong personality development, and its role in the clinical treatment of emotional disorders.
